Country of Publication: United States || The Ritual for Initiation into Consciousness (cinmayadīkṣāvidhānam) ||
We worship the Lord Mallikārjuna, the mass of consciousness, known as Channa,
the Master of devotion to the Guru, the measure, and that which transcends all qualities.
In the ancient scriptures, there are many initiations (dīkṣā) that are auspicious in nature;
yet, the difference between them lies in the extent to which they remove all limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
In the higher scriptures, she is said to be the destroyer of the three impurities;
for no distinction between those two is perceived by one who is free from limiting conditions.
Having spread the splendor of pure consciousness, which effects the identity of Śiva and the individual soul,
I shall explain that entire procedure according to the words of the Śiva-teacher.

Then, having found a disciple possessing the characteristics previously described, the teacher— having procured the ritual substances for the sacrifices at the prescribed time and in the prescribed place,
and having constructed a pavilion and so forth according to the prescribed characteristics, as follows— in verse:
The Guru should have a pavilion constructed measuring nine, five, or three cubits;
it should be known as being made of nine or five [parts] and provided with twelve pillars.
A pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed with four pillars and measuring three cubits [in width];
it is known that these pavilions should be five cubits in height.
It has four corners, four gates, and is adorned with four archways;
at its eastern side is a banyan tree, and at the southern side is a fig tree.
The best knower of ritual procedures should place an *aśvattha* tree to the north and a *plakṣa* tree as the western gateway, or he may arrange a single pit in the center.
One should arrange five [deities] in the northeast, beginning with Indra and ending with Soma;
their shapes are a square, a half-square, a half-moon, a semi-circle, and a circle.
Alternatively, one should prepare a single pit in the northeast, described as being circular;
or else, one may construct an altar (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit in size and raised by eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) using pure clay.
In a pavilion of three cubits, the altar is said to be one cubit;
when the pavilion is made five or seven cubits, an altar of two cubits should be constructed.
On a site measured at nine or eight cubits,
a pit three cubits in length and one and a half cubits in height should be prepared, resembling the surface of a mirror in its smoothness.
The secondary altar (upavedī) should be constructed measuring four finger-breadths [in width],
with a height of three finger-breadths, square, and beautiful.
Having thus constructed the pavilion, one should adorn it with banners,
as well as with appropriate canopies, fruits, sprouts, and lotuses.
Adorned with plantain trees, garlands of *darbha* grass, and mirrors—

having thus prepared [the site] on an auspicious day, under an auspicious constellation, and at an auspicious moment, in the forenoon, one should smear the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) with cow dung and other substances. When the field has been divided into twenty squares, a lotus should be drawn in the center using movable lines.
One should prepare water and sugar-cane juice, as well as a single silk cloth (*eka-paṭṭa*) and a conch-shell.

Having fashioned the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*bera*) from earth among the consecrated materials, and having prepared this mandala— which is the *gaurī-laya-liṅga-bera*— in the prescribed manner, along with colored powders, garlands, and so forth, one should worship with incense and lamps.
Having adorned himself, bathed well, and wearing white garments, having duly applied sacred ash and Rudrākṣa beads,
and having completed his daily obligatory rites, that devoted worshiper of Maheśvara, with hands purified by the general *arghya* water, sprinkles the doors with the power of mantras.

p. 3) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the *śānti*-kalā; thus in the east. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the *vidyā*-kalā; thus in the south. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the *nivṛtti*-kalā; thus in the west. Oṃ hāṃ...
"Obeisance to Pratiṣṭhā Kalādvāra"—thus, having worshipped in the north; then on the two door-posts of that [gate], from the eastward: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vināyaka."
Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vṛṣabha; oṃ hāṃ, homage to Skanda;
oṃ hāṃ, homage to Devī; oṃ hāṃ, homage to Devī; oṃ hāṃ, homage to Caṇḍā. Thus, at each door, having sprinkled water preceded by meditation and having dispelled the obstacles, [one should proceed].

Having secured the doors with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), having entered within by the western door, and having performed a circumambulation while surveying the sacrificial implements brought forward, he should protect the sacrificial hall by means of the various types of weapons and the *avakuṇṭhana* rite; thereafter, the disciple should sit upon a seat of *kuśa* grass or similar materials together with the followers of Maheśvara.

Having placed the ashes, betel-leaf, gold, and other items into a vessel, and taking that with him, he went into the presence of the Guru and said: "O Guru, O Lord! For the destruction of the suffering caused by the harsh heat, like a frog sitting in the shade of the hood of a bitten serpent to receive the Vedas for the sake of all the years."
Seated upon the shade of the hoods of the serpent of illusion, with half his body swallowed by a serpent like a dense cloud seized by a snake,
his form devoured by death, scorched by the fire of the three-fold suffering, he— possessing a body as vast as space,
desiring liberation from the fruits of merit and sin for the sake of the final rain of peace— [is thus described].
My heart, agitated by the fear of entering the machine of various wombs,
acts as a mass of foam when tasting the drops of nectar from the lotus-feet of Your Honor.

"May my compassion, which destroys all the great Indra-maya illusions, be for your grace"— having thus made this request in my presence, and having taken hold of the disciple— who stands prostrate like a staff, who is composed of pure consciousness, humble, bathed, clad in white garments, and marked with the triple ash-line (tripuṇḍra)— I [proceed].
Then, having received the betel-leaf and other offerings along with the ashes brought by the Guru, and having placed them in the midst of the Gaṇas,

he performed a prostration with eight limbs preceded by circumambulation, saying: "O lords of the Gaṇas, by your command, this disciple has come for refuge for the sake of the purificatory rite of worldly existence."

Having made a request with palms joined, saying, "I shall become a great initiate (*mahādīkṣita*); may you favor me," and being thus favored by the teacher's assent, "So be it," he should sit down. Having performed the *puṇyāha* and other rites for the sake of removing obstacles, he should thereafter perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the command of the Guru and the Gaṇas. At the outset, he should pay homage to the Triple Guṇa (*triguṇa*).
For example:
Nandīśvara, whose splendor is drawn from the son of the Mountain King (Śiva), is constantly worshipped and saluted by the gods, including Nārāyaṇa and Ka.
And Śarva stood at the gate of the inner apartments together with his attendants,
accompanied by all [his hosts], the crusher of all the Asuras.
Appointed as the presiding authority over all the Śiva-dharmas,
he is beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śiva, and possesses the glorious, supreme trident as his weapon.
Because he was attached to those who had taken refuge in Śiva, he was devoted to them even by the hundreds.
Having performed the consecration and received the command of Śiva and Śivā, may that glorious one— who has subdued his senses, is free from possessiveness, and devoid of ego— grant my desire.
Possessing the measure of the *liṅga*, he enjoys the experience of the *liṅga*;
he is the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), pleased by his own voice, and his body consists of three measures (*trimātra*).
Freed from the limiting adjuncts of power (śakti), with a beautiful smile and an auspicious countenance,
the leader of the Gaṇas named Bhṛṅgīśa is solely intent upon the worship of Śiva.
May Vīrabhadra, of great splendor and resembling a dark-blue jasmine flower or the moon, grant my desire, preceded by his favorable command.
She is eternally dear to Bhadrakālī and is the protector of the Mothers;
she is the one who severed the head of Īśa and of the wicked-souled Dakṣa.
Due to a defect in his secondary organ, he was the body-guard of the gods;
he was the illustrious attendant of Śiva and the protector of Śiva’s command.
"By the very command of Śiva and Śivā, may He grant my desire.

Having thus paid homage to the one endowed with the three qualities (*triguṇa*), and then having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), on this auspicious lunar day characterized by such specific qualities, in the illustrious [place] comprising all worlds...

Through the acceptance of the blissful form manifested by the devotion of consciousness— which consists of light and the nature of dharma established in herself— by Śiva, the Lord of the World and Śaṅkarī, who is stainless, beyond phenomenal expansion,
and seated upon the lap of Paraśiva, there arises a connection with her own ignorance.
The soul, which consists of the identification with the body composed of the fivefold elements— the product of its own independent *māyā*—

and which is bound by the chain of merit and demerit, reaches the refuge of the Guru for the sake of the Guru’s compassion; then, through the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as the door of the cage is destroyed, it becomes free from its own innate *āṇava-mala*.

The pride of being a Taijasa, which is produced by the identification with the subtle body that rests upon the impurity of Māyā, for the purpose of wearing the *bhāvaliṅga* through the initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the Vedas and other scriptures— which consist of seven divisions and serve as the cause for destroying the innate impurity of the *prājña* conditioned by the identification with the causal body.
Having observed the sevenfold distinctions of the causes for the destruction of one's own impurities, for the purpose of wearing the *prāṇaliṅga*,

and likewise for the sake of attaining the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) and the five conducts (*pañcācāra*), [one should contemplate] the words of the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

Having formed the resolve: "For the sake of accomplishing the unity of the limbs and the signs of the door of the abode of discernment (*viveka-saṃsthāna*), I shall perform the initiation consisting of consciousness (*cinmayadīkṣā*), preceded by the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-śodhana*), by means of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)," [the teacher says]:
"O disciple, having abandoned improper conduct, sit down; O disciple, I shall not speak to you until I have seen your command."
"Act in accordance with the conduct established in antiquity"—this is the instruction given through initiation (*dīkṣā*). In that regard, the *Kāmikottara* states:

"He who, having abandoned the conduct of the virtuous, persists in his own way—that man is initiated by Śiva; therefore, initiation is called 'the command' (*ājñā-dīkṣā*). Thus, one acts in accordance with the conduct established in antiquity.
Thus it is said by those proficient in the Śaiva Āgamas that these [substances] are comparable. Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

To that end: having laid out a nine-square grid upon that sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), one should say, "Homage to the square of the Śiva-principle in the center," and "Homage to the well-established vessel. Then, having filled [the vessel] with milk using the mantra *āpyāyasva*,...

Having consecrated it once with the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," [one should offer] in the east: "Obeisance to the square of the Sadāśiva-tattva; obeisance to the vessel of perfect peace. Therein, one should place curd with the mantra "Dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam" and twice with the mantra "Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe. In the south: "Obeisance to the square of the Vidyā-tattva."

Homage to the vessel possessing brilliance (*tejovatpātra*). Therein, one offers clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with the mantra "Thou art semen" (*śukram asi*) and three times with the mantra "To those who are not terrible" (*aghorebhyaḥ*). To the northern human-square (*puruṣakoṣṭha*), homage; to the vessel whose nature is nectar (*amṛtātmakapātra*), homage. Therein, one offers cow-urine with the mantra "Of that Savitṛ" (*tat savitur*) and four times with the mantra "To Vāmadeva" (*vāmadevāya*). In the west...
Salutation to the receptacle of the reality of time.

7) Salutation to the lotus leaf. There, cow dung [is applied] with the mantra "tatpuruṣāya vidmahe... and with the mantra "gandhadvārām..."; [the application of] cow dung [is performed] with the mantra "sadyojātāya...".
With the mantra, [one should prepare] the five substances, such as cow dung and so forth, by means of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāramārga*), having brought them into the state of milk;

having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so on, one should place them within the mandala. Therein, for the purpose of worshipping the vases (*kalaśa*), one should perform the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as follows:

For the consecration ceremony (*dīkṣākarma*) of this disciple, in the worship of the five jars employed therein, I choose you as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for the eastern jar. For the consecration ceremony of this disciple, in the worship of the five jars employed therein, I choose you as the officiating priest for the southern jar. For the consecration ceremony of this disciple...

"Having employed the western jar, I choose you as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); for the purpose of performing this [rite], I shall establish five jars as his disciple," thus he should resolve (*saṃkalpya*). It is as follows:
therein, within a place adorned with an eight-petaled lotus—namely, the *Aṅkuśa*.

Having prepared five altars (maṇḍalas) one above the other with *prastha*-measures of *śāli* rice, half that amount of husked rice (*taṇḍula*), and half that amount of sesame seeds; having covered them with *darbha* grass and scattered flowers upon them; there, with the mantra beginning "ā kalaśeṣu," [one should place] five water-pots (*kalaśa*) in the center, the east, south, north, and west, or in the corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*).

Having been placed in the jars, he flows; he is purified by the strainers and sprinkled; he prospers in the sacrifices that have been sown. With the verse "This prayer to Varuṇa," one pours water. Having filled [the vessel], [he recites]: "Hear this my invocation, O Varuṇa; be merciful to me today. Seeking your protection, I call upon you. "I approach you with a prayer, praising you; may you be seated."
O Varuṇa, being mindful through our oblations, be aware of us here. Do not steal away our common life, which is broad.
For we, O God Varuṇa, violate your law day by day, even as people do.

Whatever offense we humans commit against the divine folk, O Varuṇa, whether through thoughtlessness or by failing to observe thy laws, from that sin, O God, deliver us. When gamblers cheat at play, or when we speak untruths,
or when we do not know the truth— O Gods, may you all be our protectors.
At the *sthāṇvasthāma* [rite], having consecrated the water with the mantra "The waters, indeed... (*āpo vā*), [he recites]: "The waters, indeed, are all this;

the waters are all beings; the waters are the *praṇava*; the waters are cattle; the waters are food; the waters are immortality; the waters are cattle; the waters are food; the waters are immortality; the waters are the *samrāj*; the waters are the *virāj*; the waters are the *svarāj*; the waters are the *chandasa*s."

The waters are the essence of the Sāmans, the waters are the essence of the Jyotis-chants, the waters are the essence of the Yajus-formulas; the waters are truth, the waters are all the deities, the waters are *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, the waters are *om*. Having spun the thread, [he recites]:
"Spinning the thread, follow the path of light; guard the luminous steps prepared by wisdom, [making them] not loose."
With the mantra "gandhadvārām" [he offers] fragrance.

[The mantra is: "I invoke here Śrī, who has fragrance as her door, who is invincible, ever-nourishing, and the sovereign of all beings. With "ākāśāt" [he offers] unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). From space comes wind; from wind, fire.
From fire comes water; from water, the earth; from the earth, plants. "These are garments"—thus [he offers] the garment.
These are the garments, the coverings, the bestowals, the yokes, the moons, the ends, the measures, and the creations.
They have danced forth with all-sounding song. O Mitra and Varuṇa, do not withhold [them]. Toward...
p.

9) Having brought a garment, [he says]: "The child, honoring the well-yoked ones, has come to the garments, the fine clothes, and the cows of the cow; he has brought the moon-like, stainless, golden, and swift horses, O Soma."
"Dādhikrāvaraṇa" refers to curd (*dadhi*). "I have invoked the aid of the victorious, spirited steed;
may he make our mouths fragrant, and may he prolong our lives. "Madhuvātā" refers to honey (*madhu*).
"Honey for the one who follows the cosmic order (*ṛta*); the rivers flow with honey; may the plants be sweet for us; honey at night and honey at dawn."
May the earthly dust be honey-sweet; may the sky be honey-sweet; may the father be honey-sweet;
may the lord of the forest be full of honey for us; may the sun be full of honey; may our cows be honey-sweet. "Success!"—thus [he addresses] the gravel.
"Sweet [be it] for the ash that is the footprint of the knower. "Sweet [be it] for Indra, whose name is easy to invoke with the call."
"Sweet for Mitra and Varuṇa, and for Bṛhaspati; [this] honeyed [oblation], O invincible one.
"Thou art bright," [he says] regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*); "thou art bright, thou art light, thou art splendor;
[O gods,] may Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya. "Swell up," [he says] regarding the milk.
"May you swell; may your strength, O Soma, come from every side; be present at the gathering of the prize.
With the *gāyatrī* verse, "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts," one takes cow urine.
With the verse, "The door of fragrance, invincible, ever-nourished... one takes cow dung.
I invoke here Śrī, the mistress of all beings, who possesses a carriage drawn by mares.

With the verses beginning "ṛṣva" (lofty), there is the pentad concerning the skin. With the verses beginning "ṛvatibhiḥ" (with those possessing power), the Bull [Indra] is praised for his might; he is the wise one who removes our enemies with his horns. Soma, the well-doer, sits upon his own source.

Having counted [the verses], there are five sprouts (*pañcapallava*): *pra vo yajñeṣu*, *vedayanto arkaṃ*, *vyānaśīrbhiḥ*, *pṛthivīṃ na dhenubhiḥ*, and *eṣāṃ brahmāṇi*. O sages, these are peerless in their sacred power.
"May they spread out like branches upon trees. [With these words] he takes up earth, saying:

"Thou art lifted up by the boar, by the black one with a hundred arms; O Earth, destroy my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me. O Earth, thou art given by Brahmā, consecrated by Kaśyapa."

O Earth, grant me nourishment; everything is established upon you. O Earth, everything is established in you; O Earth, drive away that [evil] from me. For he [is] the jewels—thus, the jewels. For he, the well-bestowing Savitṛ, the Bhaga, is the giver of jewels. We pray for that wonderful portion. Those herbs which have been born—thus, the herbs. Those...

The plants were born for the gods three ages ago. I celebrate the hundredfold power of the *babhruṇāhya* plant, as well as its seven stations. "Soma is the chief of plants"—thus there are a hundred plants. Soma is the lord of plants; Savitṛ is the lord of instigations; Rudra is the lord of cattle; Tvaṣṭṛ is the lord of forms; Viṣṇu is the lord of mountains; and the Maruts [are the lords]...

"O lords of the hosts, may you [protect] me; O fathers, grandfathers, further ancestors, and even more distant forefathers, come hither with favor. "From joint to joint," thus [he addresses] the *dūrvā* grass: "Growing from joint to joint, from node to node, O *dūrvā*, spread forth with a thousand and a hundred shoots. "O divine essence," thus [he addresses] the *kuśa* grass.
I receive you by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan.
Having placed pure gold [into the water] with the words, "Of golden form," [he recites: "He is of golden form, being golden, [of the waters]...
May he not fall away from the golden color; may the giver of gold grant me wealth through his favor.

Regarding the phrase "those that are fruitful": this refers to fruits and flowers. "Those that are fruitful, those that are fruitless, those that are flowerless, and those that are flowering—may Bṛhaspati, the one who has brought them forth, release us from distress. From there follows the Lord (Īśāna) with the words "of all sciences" (*sarvavidyānām*).

Having invoked Īśāna into the central pitcher with the mantra [beginning with] *mantreṇa*, one should invoke Tatpuruṣa into the eastern pitcher with the mantra *tatpuruṣāya*; Aghora into the southern pitcher with the mantra *aghorebhyaḥ*; Vāmadeva into the northern pitcher with the mantra *vāmadevāya*; and Sadyojāta into the western pitcher with the mantra *sadyojātāya*.

Having performed the sixteen-fold worship (ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā), beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) for Sadyojāta, and having consecrated the five water-jars (kalaśa) with the five-syllable mantra (pañcākṣara): [one should place] the Guru in the central jar, Revanāsiddha in the eastern jar,
Maruyisiddha in the southern jar, Tārādhyam in the western jar, and [the remaining deity] in the northern jar.
"Ekorāma"— thus, with these four names of the Guru's disciples, having had the officiating priests (ṛtvij) perform the worship,
and having himself worshipped the Guru in the central pitcher, it is said: "Revaṇāsiddha is in the east, O Lord, Maruyi in the south, Paṇḍitārādhya in the west, and [the fourth] in the north."
The teachers of the Rāma [tradition] state: "One should indeed place the lords of the four directions in the pitchers, beginning from the east.
Thus is the procedure for the five pitchers according to one school. Having fashioned a pentagon, one should draw a circular mandala above it; upon that, in the form of a covering—
Having fashioned a four-cornered [mandala] with five paths using rice grains, one should draw a five-pointed [lotus] in the center, provided with a pericarp, filaments, and a circle.

Having placed a lotus and adorned it with powders of five colors, and having fashioned mandalas there with rice and other materials, one should then worship the five principles (*pañcatattva*), the five jars (*pañcakalaśa*), and the five powers (*pañcaśakti*) within the five corners. Then, taking up six jars that are pure, without cracks, and very beautiful.

In the center of one [mandala], having arranged five pitchers in the five corners and worshipped the pitchers according to the previously mentioned method, one should place the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the central pitcher and the letters from *na* to *ma* in the five pitchers. In the central pitcher is Śiva, who consists of the five Brahmans; in the five pitchers [are the other forms].

Having worshipped the five Brahmans, and having performed the ritual of the Ācāraliṅga preceded by the worship of the limbs of the devotee, and having completed the worship— this is the rite of the six pitchers. Having adopted the single-pitcher (ekakalaśa) position as maintained by the Vīraśaivas of the past,
one should construct the previously mentioned lotus-maṇḍala, take a single pitcher, and place it therein.

Having worshipped as before, having conceived [the vessel] as consisting of the five Brahmans and the five Ācāryas, and having worshipped it, one should consecrate it with the five-syllable mantra. This is the ritual for the single jar; this is the general method for the single-pakṣa [view]. Then, having constructed a mandala on the northern side of the [main] mandala.

Having adorned [the site] with colored powders, garlands, and so forth, and having placed the *tāpādra* and other items therein, one should take the Śiva-liṅga fashioned from five threads, place it in this vessel, perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
and [proceed with] the plowing and other rites for the sake of pacification on an auspicious lunar day characterized by such specific qualities, using gold...

Having bathed the Śiva-liṅga with the Anuvākas beginning with "Śṛṅgaṃ pavamānaḥ" and "Suparṇaḥ," and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) thus, the sequence of the mantras of the Anuvākas is as follows: "I take refuge in Varuṇa of the golden horn; may he grant me a sacred ford (tīrtha)."
Requested by you, [I give this]: whatever I have eaten from the unrighteous, and whatever gifts I have accepted from the wicked;
whatever evil deed I have committed with my mind, speech, or action—may Indra, Varuṇa, and Bṛhaspati [take that] upon themselves for me.
May Savitṛ purify us again and again! Homage to Agni who possesses desire; homage to Indra; homage to Varuṇa;

homage to Vāruṇī; homage to both! Whatever is cruel in the waters, whatever is impure, whatever is unappeased—let that depart from us! [Whatever has come] from overeating, from over-drinking, or from accepting a gift from a fierce person—may King Varuṇa [purify] that for us.

For one should touch [the water] with the hand while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn: "I, being sinless, stainless, liberated, and freed from evil, having ascended to the back of the firmament, shall go to the world of Brahman. And he who purifies that which is not gold—may that *Aghamarṣaṇa* [hymn] cleanse him. [And one should recite: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, and the auspicious Somaga..."
From the Sacatā, the Paruṣṇī, the Asiknī, the Marudvatī, the Vitastā, the Ājñīkī, and the Suṣomā—listen!

Order (*ṛta*) and Truth (*satya*) were born from the heat of fervor (*tapas*). From that, Night was born; from that, the ocean and the waters were born. From the ocean, the billowing sea, the year (*saṃvatsara*) was born, ordaining days and nights for all.

Having removed the wrapped cloth, one should bathe it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances while reciting the aforementioned mantras; then, having established it with scented water and worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings.

At that time, the one hundred and eight [mantras] beginning with Bhadrakālī and ending with Kālāgnibhavana were present there; indeed, the letter *kṣa* alone is the phoneme [of the end].
Starting from the word *bhava*, there are as many quarters [of verses] as there are syllables in the three mantras ending with *oṃ*.
O Śambuka, at that time, one should immediately worship the twenty-eight [deities] known as the Vratas; these are the channels named Iḍā and Piṅgalā,
as well as the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the out-breath (apāna), and the sense organs of smell and taste.
In the wind that carries the fragrance of objects, there is the pentad of qualities beginning with sound;
the earthly mandala is pale yellow, marked with a thunderbolt, heavy, elephant-shaped, four-cornered,
and fixed at three hundred million yojanas in extent.
One should cause all this to be fashioned according to the waking state, with the lotus-seated Brahmā as the appropriate cause; resembling pure collyrium,
one should place [the mantra] along the guru-line from the head down to the knees and feet.

Then, from the knees up to the navel: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Kalā of Pratiṣṭhā*. *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle (tattva) of Prakṛti*. *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Buddhi*. *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Ahaṃkāra*.
[The senses: ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hand, foot.
The anus, the generative organ, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, wind, fire, water, and earth.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the world of Śrīkaṇṭha. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the world of Umā. [The world of] Kaumāra.
The world of Vaiṣṇava; the world of Brāhma; the world of Bhairava; the world of Akṛta; the world of Īśāna; the world of Bala;
the world of Brāhma; the world of Prājeśa; the world of Saumya; the world of Indra; the world of Gandharva; the world of Rākṣasa; the world of Paiśāca;
the world of Girīśvara; salutation to the world of Sthūleśvara; the world of Śaṅkukarṇa.

The land of Kālajñāna; the land of Maṇḍaleśvara; the land of Mākoṭa; the land of Dviraṇḍa; the land of Chagalaṇḍa; the land of Sthāṇu; the land of Vraṇakṣa; the land of Bhadrakarṇa; the land of Mahābala; the land of Avimukta;
the land of Edrakoṭi; the land of Kaumāra; the land of Bhīmeśvara; the land of Mahendra; the land of Aṭṭahāsa.
Salutation to the Lord of Vimala; to the Lord of Naṭavala; to the Lord of Anākala; to the Lord of Kurukṣetra; salutation to the world of Gayā;

to the Lord of Bhairava; to the Lord of Kedāra; to the Lord of Mahākāla; to the Lord of Madyameśa; to the Lord of Āmrāntaka; to the Lord of Bilva; to the Lord of Śrīśaila; to the Lord of Hariścandra; to the Lord of Lakulīśa; to the Lord of Bhārabhūti.

Salutation to Daṇḍīśabhuvana. Oṣadhibhū, Puṣkarabhū, Naimiśāraṇyabhū, salutation to Pradhānabhuvana. Amareśabhū. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Unnata. Ḍa ḍhaṃ dha ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ, salutation to Nna. Daṃ dhaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ.

*Ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ*. Pervasive one, pervasive one! Formless one, formless one! Destroyer, destroyer! First one, first one! Splendor, splendor! Light, light! Formless, without fire, without smoke, without ash! Without beginning, manifold, manifold!
*Dhū dhū dhū dhū*! *Oṃ bhūḥ*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ*, *oṃ svaḥ*. Arising from the end and the non-end.
O Śarva, Supreme Self, Maheśvara, Great Lord, Mahādeva, Lord of True Being; O One of Great Splendor, Lord of Herbs! Release, release! First, first!

Śarva Śarva | Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva. Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the head. Oṃ hāṃ ḍaṃ, obeisance. Oṃ hāṃ vaṃ, obeisance. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gāndhārī and Suṣumnā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna. Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to the tongue and the organ of generation. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. One should perform the placement (nyāsa) in this sequence.
And it is said:
"In the [tattva] Pratiṣṭhā, one of inferior status should place the noose (pāśa), accompanied by its constituent parts (kalās)."
The principles beginning with the Prākṛta, up to the *bala*,
are recorded as twenty-three; likewise, the lineages (*vaṃśas*) and worlds (*bhuvanas*) are fifty-five in number, excluding Śrīkaṇṭha and Bhairava.
The syllables from *Amareśāntaka* to *Triśam*, along with the three additional *Nitya* syllables,
the two *Vyāpin*s, the two *Adāścaryā*s, and those ending with *Śarva*— these are declared to be the sacrificial offerings (*hutāni*) according to their respective positions.
These syllables are proclaimed as ending with *Udīhā*.

The twenty-three syllables of Vāmadeva are on the head; both [the syllables] on the odd [lines] are likewise to be worshipped with the Gāndhārī and Suṣumṇā [channels]. Then, in the organ of speech, there are the Samāna and Udāna winds, as well as the tongue and the anus.
The sense-object is taste; likewise, sound, touch, form, and taste.
Its principles are Varuṇa, its seed-syllable is white, its element is water, and its power is coolness.
Its form is like the moon, it is stationary, and its nature is white and cooling.
Joined with the Gāndhārī [channel] for thousands of millions of *yojanas*,
the hundredfold state of Sauṣuptika is the cause of the one whose banner is Garuḍa. O disciple, everything situated within extends from the navel to the knees and upward.
(The Sadguru) should place the horse there upon the cord of bonds (*pāśasūtra*).
Then, from the navel up to the heart, [he recites]: *oṃ hāṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ*...

Salutation to the principle of Māyā (māyā-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Time (kāla-tattva). Salutation to the principle of Limited Agency (kalā-tattva). Salutation to the principle of Knowledge (vidyā-tattva). Salutation to the principle of Restriction (niyati-tattva). Salutation to the principle of the Person (puruṣa-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the world of Aṅguṣṭhamātra. Oṃ hāṃ, [salutation to] the world of Īśāna; [salutation to] the world of Ekekṣaṇa.

Ekapiṅgabhu | Utsavabhu | Bhava bhava | Vāmadeva bhu | Mahāyatī bhuvanāya namaḥ | Śikhidbhu | Ekavīrabhu | Pañcāntakabhu | Śūrakabhu | Piṅgabhu | Jyotibhu | Saṃvartakabhu | Krodhabhu | Ekaśivabhu | Oṃ hāṃ Īśānabhu | Anantabhu | Tapabhu |

Umāpati-bhu | Pracaṇḍa-bhu | Ekavīra-bhu | Īśāna-bhu | Bhaveśa-bhu | Ugra-bhu | Vāma-bhu | Chaṃ Caṃ Jaṃ Jhaṃ Ñaṃ Namaḥ | Oṃ Hāṃ Oṃ Namaḥ | To Śiva, the source of all; to Śiva, whose head is Īśāna; to the face of Tatpuruṣa.

Oṃ, salutation to the one whose heart is not terrible, who has arisen from Vāmadeva, whose form consists of all beings; Oṃ Hāṃ, Oṃ, salutation! Salutation to the one who has transcended the transcendent, the protector, the deathless, the presiding authority over all yoga, the lord of all vidyās, the one whose nature is light, the Supreme Lord, the giver of boons, the conscious within the unconscious, the one in the void.
Vyomin: Oṃ hāṃ huṃ, obeisance to Aghora; Oṃ hāṃ huṃ, obeisance to Śikhā;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Unnama; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pūṣākari and Jihvikā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dhyāna and Nānā.
p.
26) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the eyes and the organ of feet. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra. One should perform the placement (nyāsa) in this manner.
Thus it has been said:
One should place that below it and know the *pāśa* (bond) to be all around it.
One should then place the seven principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *māyā* and ending with *puruṣa*.
[Recite: "Obeisance to the world the size of a thumb. Then one should meditate on the other [world] to the left.
One should place twenty-seven worlds here,
beginning with the syllable *oṃ* at the foot and ending with *vyoman* at the top;
one should know that there are twenty-one words for the *vidyā*.
The letters beginning with *vadhūkāra* and ending with *ikāra* are seven in number;
they are specifically mentioned in the *Madroghora-śikhe-droktavidyā*,
and also in the seed-syllable (*bīja*) through the bestowal of the crown (*makuṭa*), as well as *pūṣā*, *kaṭi*, and *jihvikā*.
Likewise, the Vyāna wind, the eye,
the tongue faculty, form as an object, sounds, and the qualities of touch and form;
the mandala is blood-red, triangular in shape, and characterized by the appearance of burning.

The best of gurus should place there everything— the svastika, the neck, the cloudless [vault], with millions of extensions reaching a yojana in length, the cause, the divisions of Rudra, and likewise the state of deep sleep— all of which has the brilliance of the sun.
One should touch [the body] of the disciple from the heart down to the navel.

Then, beginning from the heart up to the forehead, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śāntikalā; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śivatattva; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Īśvaratattva; [salutation] to the Śuddhatattva and Vidyātattva."

Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the world of Sadāśiva; salutation to the world of Śikhaṇḍin; [salutation] to the world of Śrīkaṇṭheśa, to the world of Trimūrti, to the world of Ekarudra, and to the world of Ekanetra.
To Śivottama-bhu; salutation to Sūkṣmeśa-bhuvana; salutation to Ananteśa-bhuvana; nanonmanī-bhu; sarvabhūtadamanī-bhu; salutation to Balapramadanī-bhuvana;
vikaraṇa-bhu; kalavikaraṇa-bhu; kālī-bhu; kaudrī-bhu; jyeṣṭhā-bhu; Oṃ Hāṃ Kaṃ.

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ gaṃ, homage! Oṃ hāṃ gaṃ, homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vyomavyāpin! Homage to the one whose form is space, who pervades all! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ananta! Homage to the Lordless One! Homage to the Lordless One, the Unsupported One! To the Pure One, the Eternal One, who is established upon the seat of yoga.

To the one eternally united with yoga, who carries away [all] through meditation: *oṃ hāṃ hoṃ*, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa; *oṃ hāṃ haiṃ*, obeisance to Aghora; *oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Bindu; *oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the letter *i*;
*oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Alambuṣā, Śoṇā, and the others; *oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Kṛkara and Kūrma.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the skin and the organs of action; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśvara. One should perform the placement (nyāsa) in this manner.
And it is said:
"One should place Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyā, Śāntā, and the triad beginning with 'Tva'."
From Sadāśiva onwards, there are the [deities] such as Vāmā, and the eighteen cities;
beginning with Vyomavyāpin, according to the path of meditation and nourishment,
the words are remembered as numbering twelve (the sun) and the syllables as zero (the sky).
In the seed-syllable, there is the drop (bindu) and the letter *a*; the mantra consists of the face and the body.
Through the *alaṃbusā* and *yaśas* channels, the winds *kṛkara* and *kūrma* [arise].
By means of these syllables, one should perform the conjunction with the wind for the distance of a *yojana*.
One should place the fourth state (turya), the infinite, and the causal Lord (Īśvara);
all this is measured by the span [of the breath] and arises from the heart through power.
"One should meditate upon the body of the child there, as well as the instructor, upon the cord of bonds.

Then, beginning from the forehead and extending to the top of the head: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the eternal Śāśvatī Kalā; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śakti-tattva; Oṃ hāṃ..."

Salutation to the one who does not depend on the world. O Bhū! O Anādyā-bhū! O Anantā-bhū! O Vyomarūpiṇī-bhū! O Vyāpinī-bhū! O Ūrdhvagā-bhū! O Mocikā-bhū! O Recikā-bhū! O Dīpikā-bhū! O Indikā-bhū! O Śāntyatītā-bhū! O Śānti-bhū! O Vidyā-bhū! O Pratiṣṭhā-bhū! O Nivṛtti-bhū! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation. Oṃ hāṃ.

Āṃ namaḥ | Iṃ īṃ u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ | Oṃ hāṃ oṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ anāthāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ huṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ kūrmāya namaḥ |
Salutation to the two *nāḍīs*, Śaṅkhinī and [Piṅgalā]. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Devadatta and Dhanañjaya.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the sense organs of hearing and speech. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva. Thus one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*).
And it has been said:

Two by two, the principles (tattvas) belonging to that [Nivṛtti-kalā] are, in sequence, of the nature of Śiva beyond [the kalās]: beginning with the powerless (adhana), the unattached (anāśrita), and Śakti, this [group] extends up to Nivṛtti. Having placed [the mantra] presiding over the navel, one should assign sixteen worlds less one.
The sound is the *praṇava*, the path, the state that is directly selfless.
The sixteen phonemes, beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*, are thus proclaimed.
One should live by means of the Īśāna-weapon, the Śivā-mantra, and likewise the Vainā;
as well as the Nāḍī, Āhvā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī, along with Devadattā and Dhanañjayā.
This has been declared and fully explained; and Sadāśiva himself is the agent.
One should meditate on the entire head as white, starting from the crest-lock (*śikhā*) up to the forehead.
Then, starting from the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*) down to the crest-lock: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *kalā* Śāntyatītottarā.
In that [place], on the arm: "Obeisance to the *nivṛtti-kalā*. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *vidyā-kalā*. Oṃ hāṃ..."

*Śāntikalāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ śāntyatītākalāyai namaḥ*. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the path of the Kalās (*kalādhvan*). *Oṃ hāṃ pṛthivī-tattvāya namaḥ*. [The principles are: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, Ether; feet, hands, speech, anus, genitals; tongue, eyes, skin, ears, mind; ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the Spirit (*puruṣa*); attachment (*rāga*), necessity (*niyati*), and knowledge (*vidyā*).
*kalā*, *kālā*, *māyā*, *śuddhavidyā*, *śakti*, and *śivatattva*: salutation to these principles (*tattvas*). This is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*).
Oṃ hāṃ! To Kālāgnibhu, Kūśmāṇḍabhu, Hāṭakabhu, Brāhmabhu, Vaiṣṇavabhu, Raudrabhu, Kapālīśabhu, Anyajabhu, Buddhabhu, Vajradehabhu, and Pramardanabhu.

Viyoktṛ-bhuvanāya namaḥ! Adharapati-bhu! Dharmapati-bhu! Nirṛti-bhu! Māraṇa-... (p. 29)

Bhu! Lakulīśa Bhu!
Hariścandra Bhu! Śrīśaila Bhu! Viśveśajitveśa Bhu! Homage to the one whose world is bowed down in reverence! (p. 30)
Salutation to Madhyameśabhū, Mahākālabhū, Kedārabhū, Bhairavabhū, Gayabhuvanāya,

saṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ kaṃ paṃ | kaṃ raṃ yaṃ maṃ bhaṃ ṣaṃ phaṃ paṃ naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ñaṃ naṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aḥ | aṃ au auṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ īṃ iṃ āṃ aṃ

Thus ends the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvā*). Oṃ, to Śiva, Oṃ, salutations, salutations! Sarva, Śarva, Śiva, Śarva; Sūkṣma, Sūkṣma; Śabda, Śabda; Jñāna, Jñāna; Piṅga, Piṅga; Pataṅga, Pataṅga; Turu-turu; Sākṣin, Sākṣin; Pūrvasthita, Apūrvasthita; Asaṃstuta, Asaṃstuta; Anarcita, Anarcita.

O you who cause the presence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all others; O source of existence who bestows happiness upon all beings; Bhava, Bhava! Śarva, Śarva! First one, first one! Release, release! O Lord of Yoga, O you of great splendor;
O Great God, Lord of True Being; O Maheśvara, O Great-Souled One; O Śarva, O Source of Śiva’s destruction, O Destruction itself!

Endless, unobstructed, heaven. Oṃ bhūḥ. Oṃ bhūḥ. Dhū dhū dhū dhūḥ. Nānā nānā. Without beginning, without ashes, without smoke, without fire, formless light, light! Splendor upon splendor! Primordial, primordial, formless. (p. 32)

O formless one, all-pervading one, pervader, conscious and unconscious, to the state of the Supreme Lord, whose form is light, the sovereign of all knowledge, the presiding authority over all yoga, the deathless protector, the most secret of secrets— *oṃ*,
salutations again and again! To the form of Sadyojāta, to Vāmadeva, the secret one, to Aghora, whose heart is non-terrible.
Obeisance again and again to Śiva, the source of all, who has the face of Tatpuruṣa,
whose head is Īśāna; to Śiva, the eternal yogin seated upon the seat of yoga, the perpetual and fixed one,
the unsupported, the lordless, the infinite, the all-pervading, whose form is space and who pervades the void.

Oṃ, salutations, salutations! Thus is the path of words (padādhva). Oṃ, salutations to Sadyojāta. Oṃ hāṃ haṃ, salutations to the Heart. Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, salutations to Vāmadeva. Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, salutations to the Head.
Oṃ hāṃ huṃ, salutations to Aghora. Oṃ hāṃ huṃ, salutations to the Tuft (śikhā). Oṃ hāṃ...
*Oṃ hāṃ haiṃ Tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ haiṃ Kavacāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ Śivāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ Śivāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ Īśānāya namaḥ*.
*Oṃ hāṃ haḥ Astrāya namaḥ*. Having thus obtained the mantras, one [should apply them] from the feet up to the crest upon the six locations.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five-syllabled *praṇava* six times. It is said: having gazed upon the disciple as the Guru, one should contemplate the body as the reality (*tattva-deha*). Having performed the placement of the six wheels (*ṣaṭ-cakra*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*), the six meditations (*ṣaḍ-adhyāna*), and the six-faced one (*ṣaḍ-ānana*) in their respective locations, one should then place the five Brahmans (*pañca-brahmāṇi*). And it is said: having constructed the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*).
(But) adorned with all ornaments,
the Ācārya sits there together with all the Māheśvaras.
To the disciple who has arrived seeking initiation, the Teacher, a treasury of compassion, should—
after the cessation of the "flesh-ball" (the physical body)— perform the transformation into the "mantra-body" through the ritual of *nyāsa*, and then cause him to ascend the *svastika*.

Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the purpose of purifying the disciple's subtle body (aṇu) through the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra), I shall perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), the smearing with ash (bhasmoddhūlana), and the wearing of ash (bhasmadhāraṇa) according to the instruction known as the Bhūtipaṭṭa," he takes the ash, places it in the palm of his left hand, and covers it with his right hand.

Having consecrated it six times with the Praṇava and the five-syllabled mantra, then, having taken the ashes while reciting the mantra "Sadyojāta," one should place them in the palm of the left hand and cover them with the right hand, [reciting] the Praṇava and the five-syllabled mantra, and the mantra "Vāmadevāya."
And with the syllable *ma* at the navel, having smeared [the area]; with the mantra "aghorebhyaḥ" and the syllable *śa* at the heart;

with the mantra "tatpuruṣāya" and the syllable *va* at the mouth; and with the mantra "īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" and the syllable *va* at the mouth, and with the mantra "īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" and the syllable *ma* at the crown of the head.
Having smeared ashes on the crown of the head with the five Brahma-mantras and the Praṇava-pañcākṣara mantra;
then, having performed the smearing of all limbs with ashes using the Praṇava-pañcākṣara mantra;
thereafter, [one should apply] ashes stirred with water upon the head with the five Brahma-mantras and the Praṇava-pañcākṣara mantra.

With the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" and the syllable *ī*, [one should worship] on the forehead; with the mantra "Tatpuruṣāya" and the syllable *va*, on the throat; [and with the mantra] "Aghorebhyo... (on the heart).

Having applied the *tripuṇḍra* marks with the mantra "iti" and the syllable "śi" on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), with the mantra "vāmadeva" on the chest, with the mantra "sadyojāta" and the syllable "na" on the right shoulder, and with the mantra [and syllable] on the left shoulder;
and having placed *rudrākṣa* beads on the locations including the crest-lock— the specific locations for each have been stated as follows.
Because one wears his mantras and so forth, as well as sacred ash (*vibhūti*), he is known as *Bhūṣṭa*. [This applies to] the stainless liberator (*anājamalamocikā*) in the measured [space].

Having generated the fire of Śiva upon that aforementioned sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or altar (*sthaṇḍila*), and then having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *praṇava* and the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*) for the purpose of establishing the [divine] digits (*kalā*) within the *liṅga*.
Having performed the *vyāhṛti* oblation and again restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*),

and for the purpose of removing the three impurities— *āṇava* and the rest— residing within the body of the disciple, having offered one hundred oblations of clarified butter as the sacrificial substance with the *praṇava* and the five-syllabled mantra, and having performed the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he then approaches the vicinity of the Guru’s mandala.

Having restrained the breaths (prāṇāyāma) and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the initiation known as Āyatta," one should take the vessel containing all the mantras composed of five threads, which has been consecrated by the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Śānteśvara;
having placed it in one's left hand and worshipped it with the threefold worship, [one says]: "O disciple, this is the well-worshipped Liṅga."

Regarding the separation [of the disciple from worldly bonds], it is said: "Having worshipped the five-threaded *liṅga* according to the prescribed rite, one should then show the *liṅga* to the disciple; this is declared by the sages to be 'dependent' (*āyatta*). At that time, having caused a curtain (*yavanikā*) to be drawn between the guru and the disciple, [one performs] the eight auspicious verses (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*) with the powder offered by the entire assembly.

Amidst the sounds of all auspicious instruments, having recited [the mantra], he—whose speech was peaceful, self-controlled, generous, and truthful, who was skillful, compassionate, and pure—[proceeded].
May this most excellent Guru— who has attained perfection through the mantra of the omniscient Śiva, who is steadfast against all adversity, who is praised by Maṇināga,
who removes the defects of a disciple’s past karma, and who bestows liberation upon the truly devoted— grant you auspiciousness, being preeminent in every virtue.
O Śiva, whose feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lord of the gods; who contains the interior of the vessel of the universe within his belly;

who is the imperishable Supreme Brahman, intent upon liberating the bound souls beginning with Brahmā; who is free from birth and death, being beyond all comparison; who bestows true splendor and liberation; and who is accompanied by Pārvatī.
May those who bring about auspiciousness grant you prosperity. || 1 ||

His body is presided over by Dharma; in every age, he is the source of the scriptures that measure Dharma and the refuge of the Vedas for the three worlds. He is the support of the sacred fords and the cosmic egg, the bringer of joy to the worlds, and the Sage praised by hosts of sages and all the immortals.
May Giriśa, whose second preeminent mountain is Nandīśa, grant you auspiciousness. || 2 ||
It wards off ghosts, spirits, piśācas, yakṣas, danujas, misfortunes, enemies, and adversaries; it obstructs the flood of poverty, diseases, fears, and evil karma.
It brings about the sevenfold excellence, happiness, merit, wealth, and the eight sovereign powers—such is its prosperity.
May those who purify the entire world bring you auspiciousness. || 3 ||
The Rudrākṣa is the subduer of the senses; its power arises from its presence at every door.

He who constantly worships the king of Rudrākṣas for the sake of benefiting all—by touching, seeing, remembering, wearing, or chanting with it—attains a merit exceeding ten million times more than that of others.
May that rudrākṣa, which bestows the fruit of infinite merit, grant you auspiciousness. || 5 ||
The great jewel that churns the depths of the ocean of the Vedas,
the essence of the meaning of the Vedas, the progenitor of the King of Mantras from which all mantras are extracted, the most meritorious among the meritorious,
the bestower of the fruits of all desires for the virtuous, and the stainless life-force of true knowledge.
May those who constantly recite the glorious five-syllabled mantra bring you auspiciousness.
May Gaṅgā, Vedavatī, Yamunā (the daughter of the Sun), Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Kṛṣṇā, and Gautamī [grant you blessings].

O wicked one! In the midst of this universe, the primary river of merit bestows the fruit of ten million billion holy baths; whatever fruit exists in all ritual acts, may that power of Śambhu’s feet, which grants eternal auspiciousness, bring you well-being.
The fruit of performing hundreds of thousands of Vedic rites— such as the thousand-fold *niyama*, the immeasurable fasts, the *prājāpatya* penance, and so forth—
is not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the merit of that infinite temple of Śiva, which possesses immeasurable palaces and instruction. That temple is infinite.
May they grant you the fruit of ten million [merits] and bestow auspiciousness upon you. || 7 ||
May there be well-being for the infinite millions of ancient great Pramatha hosts, born from the Lord of the divine Umā-liṅga whose nature is the supreme light;
for Nandīśa, who ever rejoices in bliss; for Akṣaya, Vīraka, Vīra, Bhadra, Bhadrākṣa, Mahākāla, Balapriya, Bala, Pramadana, Niṣkampa, Niṣkala, and Caṇḍakīrti.
Caṇḍeśvara, Bhṛṅgirīṭi, Mṛtyuñjaya; Dakṣa, Bhāskara, Siṃhacarmāmbaradhara,
Vyāghracarmāmbaradhara, Dharārdhanārīśvara, Hāṭakeśvara, Candragangāmbuśekhara, Vāmadeva.
To Puṣpadanta, Gaganāṇḍa, Ābharaṇa, Maṇḍābharaṇa, and all the hosts of great Pramathas;
to Ādirudra, Śāśvatarudra, Nīlarudra, Balavikaraṇarudra, Balapramathanarudra,
Śambararudra, Śarabharudra, and Mahānāṭyarudra.
To the hosts of Rudra-gaṇas headed by Rudraikapāda and Rudra; to Somasarveśvara Mahākāya, Lakulīśvara, Vṛṣabheśvara, Guhāvāsin, and the twenty-eight Yogācāryas;
to the one hundred and twelve disciples beginning with Dhamācārya; [and] to Tirunīlakaṇṭha and Tirunāllaṣovamānaka.
Jārugaṇa, Pālaniddhu, Vallabhakumārapālaka, Korbhakari, Kālacola, Kaṃnappaka, Laketa, Brahmayya, Kinnarabrahmayya, Mācidevayya, Mañcana-paṇḍita, and Śrīpati-mutthita. (p. 37)
To the assembly of preeminent ancient and modern great devotees, headed by Mallikārjuna Paṇḍita and Cannabasaveśvara,
who consist of the six fruits of devotion, Māheśvaratva, Prāsāda, Prāṇaliṅga, Śaraṇa, and Ekatva.
For the four gurus of the four ages belonging to the four monasteries beginning with Revanāsiddha, and for the lords of the Gaṇas beginning with Vīrabhadreśvara and Kumārasvāmin,

may there be well-being from all planets for the auspicious month, auspicious day, auspicious weekday, auspicious lunar mansion, auspicious yoga, auspicious karaṇa, and the excellent strength of the moon and stars at the hour of initiation for this couple.

May the two Sunakṣatras, Śubha, Ekādaśa, Sthānaphalada, Varada, Sumuhūrta, and Suprasanna be auspicious; may they remain firm! Then the Guru, together with the followers of Maheśvara, [should perform the rite] with the mantra "O King, you are firm" (dhruvante rāja), and with the mantra "Be possessed of a firm linga" (liṅgavān bhava) given by the Guru’s compassion, [he should fix it] firmly in the three corners of the triangle. [He should then remove] the curtain...
Having first perhaps propitiated [the deity] and placed auspicious unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon the head of the disciple, he recites: "May King Varuṇa establish you in firmness;
may the god Bṛhaspati establish you in firmness; may Indra and Agni establish you in firmness; may they uphold the kingdom in firmness.
Then, at an auspicious moment, having removed the curtain, the Guru, facing north, [proceeds].

Having seated the disciple facing east upon his own seat to the left of himself, the Guru then performs the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and makes the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall perform the initiation (dīkṣā) for the disciple known as [Name]. Then, having covered both himself and the disciple with silk or similar fine cloth, he proceeds thereafter with the disciple.
Having stirred his left hand seven times and having consecrated it with the root mantra,
he should firmly grasp Śānteśvara— worshipped in his own left hand— with his own right hand and the left hand of the disciple.
And it is said:
"The preceptor should worship the disciple's left hand seven times;
having placed the worshipped *liṅga* there, he should grasp it firmly. And it is further said: "Having grasped it, the teacher..."
"One should move the *liṅga* from the head and other parts [of the body] by means of the *avadāna*; thus the *liṅga* is said to be under one's own control.

Then the Guru, having performed his own worship and having stirred his own right hand, consecrates it six times with the *praṇava* and the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*), thereby fashioning the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*). O—

O disciple, having abandoned the delusion regarding the eighteen *kulas*, create the realization within the *Śaraṇakula*. O disciple, having cast aside the body, the senses, the physical frame, and the rest of worldly existence, contemplate thus: "This is indeed my fivefold conduct (*pañcācāra*) in the worship of Śiva. O disciple, do not let your mind be agitated by the many impurities of the three *malas*. O disciple, that one [reality] alone—
Speak correctly regarding the state that consists of twenty-five principles and the state that consists of ten principles.

Become one who is united with the Liṅga and the Aṅga. O disciple, you are the Liṅga; you are its very essence. O disciple, you are Paraśiva himself; you become the nature of the six Liṅgas and Aṅgas. O disciple, you are of the nature of Brahman, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss.

And so, having thus instructed [the disciple] regarding the pledges (*samaya*) and so forth through the seven initiations (*dīkṣā*), he places the "Hand of Śiva" upon the head of the disciple with the mantra: "This hand of mine is the Blessed One; this hand of mine is the most blessed; this hand of mine is the universal remedy; this is the touch of Śiva; this is the mother... [this hand of mine].
This father has come as a life-giver; this is your path forward.
O Subandhu, look out! And it is said: having abandoned wandering through the eighteen families, [attain liberation] through union with Śiva.

One should always maintain love for the Śaraṇa as if it were one's own home; this is the initiation (dīkṣā) of Śambhu known as Samaya. Having abandoned the body, senses, house, and so forth, as well as worldly existence (saṃsāra), one should practice the conduct of worshipping Śiva; this is the initiation called Niḥsaṃsāra. "Worldly existence" refers to that which is constant. This is the initiation known as Niḥsaṃsāra.
She is the unadorned one of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

That which does not exist within the threefold state of existence due to a corrupted mind—this is called the Great Initiation (*mahādīkṣā*), known as the Great Goddess of Departure (*niryāṇa-maheśvarī*). From that, the state of liberation (*mukti*) consists of five; the state of the inauspicious (*aśiva*) consists of twenty and ten.

That which the Lord always effects through the union of the *liṅga* and the *aṅga* is declared to be the true initiation (*tattvadīkṣā*), which brings about union with Śiva. This indeed is what constitutes the state of being a *liṅga*, and not merely by the title of "Teacher" (*deśika*).
This initiation, known as the "Self," is directly of the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*).
Being himself Paraśiva, he is the very embodiment of the *liṅga* and the body;
this supreme initiation is called the "summoning of the celestial planets."

"This [Self] is declared to be Śrī Saccidānanda-Brahman; this initiation, known as Satya-śuddhā, brings about all auspiciousness. Having thus performed the Vedic initiation, O Guru, having meditated upon the Śiva-Śāmbhavī state which stands above all principles (tattvas) within your own being, and thereafter, by beholding that [state], you shall proceed to bestow [the initiation].

O disciple, you have not yet realized the Reality that is beyond the *iṣṭaliṅga*; therefore, extend [your consciousness] as far as your own body, which is like a tree. With the realization that "I am the Lord of the disciple-liṅga," perform the worship of the relationship between cause and effect in the *iṣṭa* and other [liṅgas]. O disciple, do not commit any offense against living beings on the path. O disciple!
p.

40) "I am that Supreme Śiva, devoid of beginning, middle, and end"—establish yourself in this conviction. O disciple, effect the dissolution of all states within this *liṅga*. O disciple, having thoroughly understood and offered up all this, [become] free...

"Being in a state of doubt, set it right. Having thus instructed [the disciple] through the seven initiations beginning with one-pointedness of mind, and having recited the mantra "Bring [the mind] within the vital breaths by means of the mind," according to the word of Śiva, he should invoke the subtle body (*liṅga*) of the mind within the vital breaths— wherein there is anger, thirst, and forbearance— and having meditated upon that thirst, [he should sever] the cause.
Having understood the root of the net, and having reflected upon it and established it, they say that Rudra is the one in the firmament.

We praise the eternal, ancient Rudra with our speech, O Giriśa; may he be well-disposed toward us so that this entire world may be free from misfortune. Then, [the teacher speaks] into the right ear of the disciple.
Having slowly taught the Praṇava and the five-syllabled mantra three times, it is said:
"There is no reality higher than the chosen Liṅga; this single-pointed initiation (ekāgra-dīkṣā) dries up the ocean of worldly existence.
Because it does not release its hold until the very end of the body-tree, behold this initiation known as 'the firm' (dṛḍha-pratijñā)."
With the realization "I am Satī, the mistress of the Liṅga," who takes pride in being the essence of the Liṅga, one should always offer up the body, the senses, and one's inner disposition.
Free from longing, one should perform sacrifices and other rites directed toward the Liṅgas.

Following the application of the name of initiation known as the "Worship of the Five Senses," one speaks of living beings without fault; this is performed with reverence and without envy. The teachers, the masters of Śiva, call this the practice known as non-violence (ahiṃsā).
The supreme Śiva is not separate from the beginning, middle,
and end; this very state, expressed as "I am He" (*so'ham*), is indeed the innate form of the embrace (*aliṅgana*).
The dissolution of one's state within that *liṅga* is indeed initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is the dissolution of the mind. Having bound all this together and known it, one becomes free from doubt;
one immediately abides in the supreme refuge of the initiation of the intellect (*buddhi-dīkṣā-mahottarā*).
Having thus performed the preliminary initiation (*anudīkṣā*), the Guru, by his own nature, mentally unites the disciple with the previously mentioned state of being;

having seen him, he places that portion [of the disciple]—marked by the seal formed by the palm of the left hand—with the root-mantra, according to the rule of the indefinite eightfold [application]. And it is said:

Having taken the form of the Guru and placed a digit (kalā) upon the head of the disciple, by means of his own true being alone, he made the digit of the Nīlalohita [deity] manifest. As is the digit, so is the disposition; as is the disposition, so is the mind.

As the mind is, so is the vision; as the vision is, so is the ground. Just as oil exists within the water, the jar, the tip, and the true devotion, so too does the supreme Śāmbhavī power abide, pervading the body, the vital breath, and the self.
Having the brilliance of a blazing fire at the end of time and a radiance equal to ten million suns,
the supreme *akalā*— whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*)— is situated above him, reaching to the very tip of his crest.
It is not merely the sky, but the most subtle, the supreme awakener of all principles (*tattva*).

Having drawn her forth according to the prescribed rule, one should seat her upon the *liṅga*, having addressed the Deity thus: "O Paraśiva, whose nature is both moving and unmoving, do not become [separate];

O you who have the body of a single devotee, instruct the devotee. Then, addressing the disciple: "O you who possess the vital breath of *bhūti*, you who possess the vital breath of the *bhava-liṅga*..."
Having thus instructed him, and then having given the water for the feet and the prasāda, he says to the humble disciple, "Worship the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama correctly. (p. 42)
"O you who possess the eightfold enclosure (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*), place your faith in every way and engage yourself in the five conducts (*pañcācāra*). And it is said:

having spoken thus to the humble disciple—"Worship properly the *prāṇodaka*, the *prasāda*, the *guru-liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama*s"—[he says], "Place your faith in every way in the eightfold enclosure."
Entrust [these] to the five preceptors.
And it is said:
"The water for washing the feet, the grace, and the Guru’s mobile liṅga."

Mantra, rudrākṣa, and sacred ash constitute what is known as the eightfold enclosure (aṣṭāvaraṇa). Furthermore, the conduct of the liṅga, the conduct of the virtuous, the conduct of Śiva, service to the guru, and the letter ‘ca’— these are remembered as the fivefold conduct (pañcācāra).

Then, having covered the *liṅga* with a fine garment such as one made of Kāśī cloth, the disciple, with his own voice, should hold the tip of the *brahmagranthi* while reciting the verse beginning with the mantra: "Oṃ namo brahmaṇe dhāraṇam. [The mantra is: "Oṃ namo brahmaṇe dhāraṇaṃ me astu nirākaraṇaṃ dhārayitā bhūyāsaṃ karṇayośśatam."
One should not be arrogant. [Recite: "Om, of me, of such-and-such a person. Therein, one should instruct him in the rules of conduct and so forth.

One should avoid whatever substance has fallen within his field of vision. One should offer pure substances and the various types of food to the *liṅgas*. Thus, the Vīraśaiva disciple is consecrated, being fully endowed with the vows.

The general vow for the Vīras and Mahā-Īśvaras is declared: regarding the previously mentioned Śiva-mudrās and their bearers in every respect, O wise one, one should practice devotion even at the cost of wealth or life;
one must never commit any sin against them oneself.

If a sin has been committed through a boon, one should not overlook it by means of the three instruments [of body, speech, and mind]. For if one is weak when strength is failing, one should proceed toward that which is secure.
If one is devoid of the instruments [of action], one should not fix the intellect upon them;
for just as the *liṅga* is made twofold by initiation through the Guru and wealth,
so too is there the unity of the *liṅga* from that point forward through the yoga of inseparable connection.
Having established it through the vital breath of the body, one should deposit it into the *prāṇaliṅga*.
One should not allow these two—the vital breath and the body—to become separated from one another.
One should wear the *liṅga* bestowed by the Guru with constant mindfulness.

If the *liṅga* falls due to negligence, one should even give up one's life. That lowest of men who maintains his life-breaths when the *prāṇaliṅga* has fallen should be known as a *caṇḍāla*; he is a traitor to Śiva and others should not touch him.
If the vow of the *prāṇaliṅga* is violated, one should strike the hand with a sword;
one should cut the face like a lotus, possessing the characteristic marks of a servant.
Thus declared in the *Vīraśaiva-krama*, it is exempt from [ordinary] expiation.
Having thus instructed in the form of a command, one should worship one's own chosen *liṅga* once, twice, or thrice a day. It has been said: "One should worship once, twice, or thrice a day.
Then the disciple should practice the *praṇava* mantra for his gurus.
Having worshipped the preceptor, one should then cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given; cows, land, gold, and many other implements should be presented to the teacher with faith and devotion.
Then, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given to all the officiating priests who possess knowledge;
one should feed the devotees of Śiva and honor them with betel leaves.
One should perform worship of the Guru and feed [him] immediately thereafter.
This supreme procedure for initiation, which embodies all principles (tattvas), has been proclaimed.
May I always attain Śiva-rātri and the Great Time (Mahākāla) arising from the Liṅga.
During the night, for fourteen ghaṭikās, when the moon is full, O Six-faced One, listen to what the wise say: the waning moon is not to be marked [for fasting].
This applies even on Śivarātri, at the time of a saṃkrānti, and during the five parvan days.
One should abandon all defects regarding the lunar day, asterism, weekday, and so forth.
Having performed the installation of the deity, the instruction for wearing [the amulet] is given by the preceptor.
O Six-faced One, listen briefly to the procedure for the performance of the vow, my child.
The act of naming transcends qualities, yet it is accompanied by qualities that possess attributes.
[One should worship] Sadāśiva, Mahādeva, the destroyer of great sins.
By what fault could there be any offense against the Blessed One, for he is indeed the lord of all deities?
Therefore, during a festival, at an auspicious time, when the day or lunar mansion is not unfavorable,
or on Śivarātri and all such occasions— on these festive times, the wise one should perform the installation according to the prescribed rite for the virtuous.
Indeed, O Goddess, these are known as the great defects of Dharma.
|| Salutations to Sāmbaśiva ||
